entities.context: Abstract. This study examines the trajectory of two captive groups taken after the defeat of the AD 450–1 Armenian rebellion against Sasanian King Yazdgerd II and argues that the destinations and treatment of these captives must be understood in terms of their social positions, as well as when they were taken captive and the part they played in the rebellion. Sasanian authorities carefully delineated between the treatment of children, secular nobility, and Christian clerics involved in the rebellion, aiming both to regain control of the rebellious region and prosecute other defensive objectives along the empire’s northern border.

entities.context: The captives of Khuzestan comprised Vahan Mamikonean, his younger brothers Vasak and Artašēs, an unspecified number of children from other clans (including the related Kamsarakan family), and Bishop T‘at‘ik of Basean. He depicts the children being taken from their wet-nurses (dayeakk‘), although this does not necessarily signify they were infants, as dayeak could refer to more long-term childrearing or educational arrangements that sometimes continued until adulthood.
